pages.x: After the Persian wars, Athens led a league of island and coastal cities and turned it into an empire paid for by their tribute. Sparta, a land power ruled by a warrior class, feared it. The historian Thucydides said the war came from the rise of Athens and the fear it caused in Sparta.

Pericles, Athens's leading statesman, had a plan: let the Spartans burn the farms of Attica while everyone sheltered behind the Long Walls that joined Athens to its port, and let the navy raid the enemy coast. In his speech for the first dead, he praised Athens as a school for all of Greece.

In 430 BC a plague broke out in the crowded city. Thucydides caught it and lived, and described the fevers, the bodies piled in temples and people giving up all law and decency. Perhaps a quarter of the people died, Pericles among them.

In 415 BC Athens sent a great fleet to conquer Syracuse in Sicily, urged on by the brilliant, reckless Alcibiades, who then went over to Sparta. The expedition ended in total defeat: thousands of Athenians were captured and left to die in the stone quarries of Syracuse.
Even in wartime Athens laughed at itself. In Aristophanes' comedy Lysistrata, staged in 411 BC, the women of Athens and Sparta go on strike and refuse their husbands until the men make peace.

Persian gold paid for a Spartan fleet under Lysander, who caught the Athenian ships pulled up on a beach at Aegospotami in 405 BC and took almost all of them. Cut off from its grain, Athens starved and surrendered in 404, and its Long Walls were pulled down to the music of flute girls.

The war wore out the Greek cities and left them open to Macedon a few decades later. Thucydides's history of it, written to last for all time, is still read by generals and diplomats for what it says about power, fear and war.
pts: Ended the golden age of Athens
Told by Thucydides, the first great war historian
